questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: The question an observational study cannot answer
questions.learningObjective: Identify the causal claim an observational study cannot support
questions.stem: Ticket 42 asks whether the new checkout flow caused signups to rise; the data come from users who chose to switch, so which causal question is out of reach?

options.text: Whether the new flow would raise signups if randomly assigned to all users
Whether switching was associated with higher signups
options.misconception: treats an observed association as already causal

options.text: Whether the new flow raised signups among those who chose it
options.misconception: confuses association within self-selected users with a causal effect

options.text: Whether switchers differed from non-switchers at baseline
options.misconception: answers a descriptive question instead of the causal one

questions.explanation: An observational study can describe associations and baseline differences, but it cannot answer what would happen under random assignment. The tempting wrong idea is that association among choosers implies causation.
questions.hint: Ask what random assignment would change.

options.text: Only the variables recorded in the ticket
options.misconception: limits balance to observed covariates only

options.text: Both observed and unobserved baseline differences
Only the outcome measured after treatment
options.misconception: confuses post-treatment balance with baseline balance

options.text: The sample sizes of the two arms

questions.explanation: Random assignment balances all baseline differences in expectation, including unmeasured ones. The tempting wrong idea is that only recorded covariates get balanced.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What one matched pair is
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a matched pair represents
questions.stem: Ticket 11 pairs each treated user with one control user of the same region and tenure; in one sentence, what does that single matched pair represent?

answer.exemplar: A matched pair is two units with similar observed covariates, used to estimate the treatment effect by comparing like with like while holding those covariates fixed.

questions.explanation: A matched pair links comparable units so the contrast isolates treatment rather than baseline differences. The tempting wrong idea is that pairing removes all confounding including unmeasured.
questions.hint: Pair like with like on observed traits.

The main effect of notifications averaged over layouts

The pooled variance of the four cells

questions.subject: STATISTICS

questions.learningObjective: Compute the standard error of a difference in two means
questions.stem: Ticket 31 has two arms with standard deviations 6 and 8 and 25 users each; what is the standard error of the difference in means?
questions.explanation: SE equals sqrt(6^2/25 + 8^2/25) equals sqrt(36/25 + 64/25) equals sqrt(100/25) equals 2. The tempting wrong idea is to pool the standard deviations first.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a two-sample t statistic
questions.stem: Ticket 35 compares mean response times of 4.2 and 3.7 with standard error 0.25; what is the test statistic and what does it measure?

answer.exemplar: The t statistic is (4.2 - 3.7)/0.25 = 2.0, measuring how many standard errors the observed difference is from zero under the null.

questions.explanation: Divide the difference by its standard error. The tempting wrong idea is to divide by the raw standard deviation instead.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a pooled standard deviation
questions.stem: Ticket 39 has two arms of 10 each with sample standard deviations 4 and 6; what is the pooled standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Pooled variance equals ((9*16)+(9*36))/18 equals (144+324)/18 equals 26, so pooled SD equals sqrt(26) about 5.1. The tempting wrong idea is to average the two standard deviations.

The smaller of n1-1 and n2-1

questions.topic: Test statistic for a difference in two means
questions.learningObjective: Compute a two-sample t statistic
questions.stem: Ticket 15 compares mean response times of 5.0 and 4.4 with standard error 0.3; what is the test statistic and what does it measure?

answer.exemplar: The t statistic is (5.0 - 4.4)/0.3 = 2.0, measuring how many standard errors the observed difference is from zero under the null.

questions.explanation: Divide the difference by its standard error. The tempting wrong idea is to divide by the raw standard deviation.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Pooled standard deviation for two equal arms
questions.learningObjective: Compute a pooled standard deviation
questions.stem: Ticket 19 has two arms of 10 each with sample standard deviations 3 and 5; what is the pooled standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Pooled variance equals (9*9 + 9*25)/18 equals (81+225)/18 equals 17, so pooled SD equals sqrt(17) about 4.12. The tempting wrong idea is to average the two standard deviations.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
questions.learningObjective: Identify when Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom apply
questions.stem: Ticket 23 compares two arms with unequal variances and unequal sizes; which degrees of freedom should be used?

options.text: The larger of n1-1 and n2-1

options.misconception: uses pooled df when variances are unequal

options.text: The smaller of n1-1 and n2-1

questions.explanation: Unequal variances call for the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation. The tempting wrong idea is to pool degrees of freedom regardless.
questions.hint: Match df to the variance assumption.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Paired t statistic from within-pair differences
questions.learningObjective: Compute a paired t statistic
questions.stem: Ticket 27 has 25 pairs with mean within-pair difference 4 and standard deviation of differences 10; what is the paired t statistic?

options.misconception: uses raw difference SD as SE

questions.explanation: SE equals 10/5 equals 2, so t equals 4/2 equals 2.0. The tempting wrong idea is to use the raw standard deviation of differences.
questions.hint: Divide the difference SD by sqrt(n).

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Design effect of a clustered allocation
questions.learningObjective: Compute a design effect for clustering
questions.stem: Ticket 31 allocates by cluster with 20 users per cluster and intraclass correlation 0.03; what is the design effect?
questions.explanation: Design effect equals 1 plus 19 times 0.03 equals 1.57. The tempting wrong idea is to multiply ICC by cluster size without subtracting one.
questions.hint: Use 1 plus (cluster size minus one) times ICC.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Standard error from the number of clusters
questions.learningObjective: Recognize that precision depends on cluster count
questions.stem: Ticket 35 has many users but only 12 clusters; standard error is driven mainly by which quantity?

options.text: Total number of users across clusters
Number of clusters, not total users

questions.explanation: In a clustered design, the number of clusters drives precision. The tempting wrong idea is that more users within clusters add independent information.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Main effect in a two-by-two factorial
questions.learningObjective: Compute a main effect in a two-by-two factorial
questions.stem: Ticket 39 has cell means 8, 12, 10, 14 for factors A and B; what is the main effect of A?
questions.explanation: Main effect of A equals ((8+12)/2) minus ((10+14)/2) equals 10 minus 12 equals -2, magnitude 2. The tempting wrong idea is to compare single cells instead of averaging.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Interaction contrast in a two-by-two factorial
questions.learningObjective: Compute an interaction contrast
questions.stem: Ticket 43 has cell means 8, 12, 10, 14; what is the interaction contrast?
questions.explanation: A effect at B low equals 4; at B high equals 4; interaction equals 0. The tempting wrong idea is to difference the wrong diagonal.
questions.hint: Compare the simple effects of A across B levels.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Error degrees of freedom in a replicated factorial
questions.learningObjective: Compute error degrees of freedom in a replicated factorial
questions.stem: Ticket 47 has a two-by-two factorial with 4 replicates per cell; how many error degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: Error df equals 4 cells times (4 minus 1) equals 12. The tempting wrong idea is to use total n minus 1.

questions.topic: A design feature that undercuts a causal claim
questions.learningObjective: Identify a design feature that undercuts causality
questions.stem: Ticket 51 compares users who opted into a beta against non-opt-ins with no randomisation; which design feature most undercuts a causal claim?

options.text: The beta lasted only two weeks

questions.explanation: Self-selection confounds treatment with motivation. The tempting wrong idea is to blame sample size or duration.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Reading a combination of two treatments
questions.learningObjective: Read a combination of two treatments
questions.stem: Ticket 55 shows a factorial where push plus new layout raises conversions more than either alone; how do you read that combination?

options.text: As random noise in the cells
As a pure main effect of push
As a main effect of layout only
As synergy between the two treatments

questions.explanation: A combined effect beyond the sum of parts indicates synergy. The tempting wrong idea is to attribute it to one factor.
questions.hint: Combined beyond the sum suggests interaction.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What a crossover design still risks
questions.learningObjective: Identify the risk a crossover design still carries
questions.stem: Ticket 59 uses a crossover where each user gets both flows in sequence; what risk remains even with random order?
questions.explanation: Carryover effects from the first treatment can persist into the second period. The tempting wrong idea is that random order removes all carryover.
